post_text: Across the Soviet Union, the exchange "Where?" "In Karaganda!" was a punchline about the middle of nowhere. The city, on the steppe of central Kazakhstan, now has a monument to the joke and about half a million residents. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Coal. It was found here in the 1800s, credited to a shepherd, though who found it first is disputed. In the late 1920s Soviet planners drafted a dozen mines and a city to serve them. They also set up Karlag, a prison camp network built to supply the mines with slave labor.

3/ Deportees built it too. Two or three families shared a dugout, heated with weeds and dried dung. Cold, scurvy and typhus caused mass deaths in 1931–33. By the 1940s up to 70% of residents were ethnic Germans. Over 100,000 people have since emigrated to Germany.

4/ Coal still keeps it going. 8 mines remain of up to 26 in Soviet times, and the city's water comes by canal from the Irtysh River, more than 400 km away. Methane makes the work deadly. In October 2023 a fire at the Kostenko mine killed at least 32 people.

post_text: Ghadames gets 73 mm of rain a year and July highs around 41°C, and for most of its history it drank from a single spring. It's an oasis town in northwestern Libya, near the Algerian and Tunisian borders. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The reason is a spring, Ain al-Faras: 'the only source of life,' one study calls it. Its water was split among seven clans on a strict schedule, timed by a pierced cup called the gâddous, via five canals proportioned 1:3:9:27:81. The community still manages it.

3/ Water made it a stop; trade made it rich. From Arab rule until the 19th century it sat at a junction of caravan routes. Caravans from the south brought slaves, gold, ivory and ostrich feathers, and its traders reached Timbuktu. When that trade vanished, the town declined.

4/ The old mud town is almost fully roofed over: supplies downstairs, families above covered alleys, linked rooftops reserved for women as their own streets. People moved to new houses outside. No one lives in it year-round, but many return in summer to escape the heat.

post_text: Its Inuktitut name, Aujuittuq, means "place that never thaws." The average yearly temperature is −16.5 °C. Grise Fiord, on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, is Canada's northernmost civilian community, with 144 people at the 2021 census. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Because Canada put them there. In 1953 the government moved Inuit families from Inukjuak (then Port Harrison), Quebec, to the High Arctic. They were promised homes and plentiful caribou. They found no buildings and were told to take one caribou per family per year.

3/ They were told they could go home if they wished, after one year or after two or three, depending on the account. The offer was later withdrawn. The motive is disputed: the government calls the move humanitarian; many argue it was about Cold War Arctic sovereignty.

4/ Families learned the beluga routes and stayed. In 2010 Canada apologized. In Grise Fiord, a statue of a woman, a boy and a husky gazes toward Resolute Bay, where other relocated families were sent. In Resolute, a statue of a lone man looks back.

post_text: In July 1983 the air here fell to −89.2 °C, the lowest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth. The air holds as little oxygen as the top of Mount Elbrus. Vostok Station is a Russian base 3,488 m up on the East Antarctic ice sheet. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The Soviets built it in 1957 because of what lay nearby: the South Geomagnetic Pole, where Earth's magnetic axis meets the surface, a good spot to study the ionosphere and magnetic storms. But magnetic poles wander. By 1996 it was about 100 km away.

3/ The real prize was underneath. A core drilled with the French stopped at 3,623 m in 1996 and held 420,000 years of climate history, across four previous glacial periods. Below it lies Lake Vostok, 14,000 sq km, under about 4 km of ice. Drillers reached it in 2012.

4/ Newcomers lose 5–10 kg in their first month. Rescue is impossible eight months a year. In April 1982 the generator shed burned and chief mechanic Aleksei Karpenko died trying to save it. The rest wintered huddled in a small hut, heated by wicks dipped in diesel.

post_text: A Low German-speaking Mennonite town in the Belize jungle, reached partly by a hand-cranked ferry, produces the country's only commercial milk and pumps its only oil. Spanish Lookout, Cayo District, Belize. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ They had moved before. Dutch-Russian Mennonites, they settled in Canada in the 1870s and Mexico in 1948. Then Mexico couldn't promise their sons draft exemption and wouldn't sell them much more land. In March 1958 the first group landed in British Honduras.

3/ George Price wanted Belize less dependent on its neighbours. The deal: their own churches and schools, with their own teachers, in exchange for BZ$500,000 of investment and paying every cost of settling. They started in jungle, with a tree as the church.

4/ The settlement, 3,108 people in 2022, now has Western Dairies, Belize's only commercial milk producer, and reportedly its largest chicken and egg suppliers. It also has Belize's only oilfield, past its 5,000-barrel-a-day peak and nearing its economic limit around 2030.

post_text: In 1973 a volcano erupted on Heimaey, a small island off Iceland's south coast. Lava crushed half the town and headed for the harbour. Everyone left overnight, mostly on fishing boats. Then many came back. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The harbour. Cliffs shelter it, and extremely rich fishing grounds lie minutes away, beside cliffs full of nesting seabirds. Tradition says Herjólfur Bárðarson settled here about 900; a 1971 dig found settlement nearly a century earlier.

3/ It still pays. The Westman Islands hold about 2% of Iceland's people and land 15% of its catch. Fish come ashore and into processing almost immediately. The largest employer, Vinnslustöðin, was started on the last day of 1946 by 105 local fishermen.

4/ So in 1973 they fought for the harbour, spraying the lava with six million tons of seawater until it hardened and turned aside. It worked. One man died. Islanders came back, dug out their houses and heated them with the lava. The island grew from 11.2 to 13.44 km².

post_text: Long before anyone called it Free Town, Portuguese traders used stone steps carved by the shore to load enslaved Africans onto ships. The city later built on that ground is Freetown, capital of Sierra Leone. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ In 1787 the abolitionist Granville Sharp picked the site as a haven for London's 'Black Poor'. They bought land from a Koya Temne chief, though some historians doubt the Koya saw the sale as permanent. In 1789 his successor, King Jimmy, burned the settlement.

3/ The lasting town came from Nova Scotia: Black Loyalists tired of cold, racism and slow land grants, promised full rights and 30+ acres. 1,196 sailed from Halifax in January 1792. In the usual account, men cleared jungle to a cotton tree and everyone marched there singing.

4/ Freetown grew as the Royal Navy, enforcing the slave-trade ban, landed 50,000 to 70,000 freed Africans here, and its harbour still drives the city. They entered through the King's Yard Gate, inscribed: "any slave who passes through this gate is declared a free man."

post_text: No road reaches Iquitos, the largest city in the Peruvian Amazon. Its one highway runs about 100 km to the town of Nauta and stops. The nearest town on Peru's road network is nine days upstream by boat. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Because Peru put a port here on purpose. After an 1851 deal with Brazil opened the Amazon to free navigation, three navy steamers, the Pastaza, Próspero and Morona, arrived on 5 January 1864. A dockyard imported from England went up immediately.

3/ The 1880–1914 rubber boom brought an opera house, mansions and a synagogue founded by Moroccan Jews. It also brought slavery: Julio César Arana's company kept indigenous workers in near bondage, and captured children were sold in town for £20–£50.

4/ Asian plantations grown from smuggled seeds killed the boom in the 1910s. Iquitos kept growing anyway, on mahogany, then oil found in the 1960s, then tourism. Ocean-going ships still sail up the Amazon to it, and unload for hours with rusty manual cranes.

post_text: Port Arthur was chosen because it was hard to leave. For 47 years this convict settlement on Tasmania's Tasman Peninsula held men who kept reoffending after being transported to Australia: "a prison within a prison." Today 247 people live there. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ It began in 1830 as a timber camp, and the land did the guarding. The peninsula is ringed by water the authorities said was full of sharks. Escape on foot meant crossing Eaglehawk Neck, 30 metres wide, past soldiers and a line of chained dogs kept to bark, not bite.

3/ At night, lamps on chest-high posts lit the dog line, with cockle shells scattered below to reflect the light. Some dogs hadn't been off the chain in years. If a man got past, semaphore stations could get word to Hobart in about 10 minutes.

4/ The prison closed in 1877, and the town got by on timber and fishing. Then the visitors came. Now the prison is the industry: 333,068 visitors in 2023–24, 199 staff at the site, and about a third of the 247 residents working in museum operation.

post_text: Cassidy, on Vancouver Island just south of Nanaimo, once held what was called 'the best company town in Canada': arc-lit paved streets, steam-heated lockers. In 1936 it was auctioned off and carted away. About a thousand people live there anyway. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The place is named for Thomas Cassidy, who farmed here from the 1870s. Its coal wasn't for the island. Copper firm Granby bought the local coal company in 1917 and began mining in 1918 to make coke for its copper smelter at Anyox.

3/ To head off labour unrest, Granby built lavishly: arc-lit paved streets, a theatre, a 76-room concrete dormitory with steam heat, steam-heated lockers for miners' clean clothes. Below ground the mine was wet and prone to gas blowouts. It still had a waiting list for jobs.

4/ In 1932 the seam ran out, the Depression hit and the Anyox smelter shut. One watchman guarded the empty town for years. In 1936 it was auctioned off. Logging, then Nanaimo commuters, refilled the area. Nanaimo's airport sits on land Cassidy's son sold the military in 1942.

post_text: In 1920 a British colonel drew a border along a small stream through the middle of this town. Estonia got the station and most of the centre. Latvia got the suburbs. That's Valka, Latvia, twin of Estonia's Valga. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The name comes from a portage: "valks" meant where boats and cargo were dragged from the Gauja basin to the Pedele. It grew late, with a teachers' seminary and a railway junction: 4,200 people in 1881, over 20,000 by the end of WWI.

3/ In November 1917 the decision to proclaim an independent Latvia was made here, and its flag first flew here. The town, about half Estonian and half Latvian, was claimed by both. Colonel Tallents's line satisfied neither, and with minor changes it is still the border.

4/ Since Schengen in 2007 the fences are gone. Wages are higher in Estonia. About 1,000 Latvians are registered in Valga Municipality, and one Valga flat in five, an estate agent says, goes to a Latvian buyer. In one year, 82 Latvian babies were born on the Estonian side.

post_text: Until 1982, the houses in Blacks Harbour, a village on New Brunswick's Bay of Fundy, belonged to a sardine company. So did the land, the stores and most of the jobs. When the village got its own council in 1972, the company kept the water. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Herring. In 1885 the Connors brothers started canning on the harbour: clams, chowder, berries. Sardines followed in 1889. Workers bought on credit at the company store, and the bill came out of their wages. The company farm supplied their beef and milk.

3/ In 1923 the cannery ran only in summer, and its workers camped in tents and tarpaper shanties. Then Alan and Neil McLean bought the company, added can-making and box-making machinery for winter work, and built homes, schools, hospitals and a police department.

4/ Cooke Aquaculture began here as a family salmon farm and now has 15,000 employees worldwide. In 1950 Connors packed 490 million sardines into 70 million tins. At peak season its workforce reached up to 3,600. The 2021 census counted 907 people in the village.

post_text: Kili has no harbor and no lagoon. Ships can't reach it four months a year, and one contractor had to surf equipment ashore. Several hundred people live on this 200-acre island in the Marshall Islands. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ They didn't choose it. In 1946 the US moved Bikini Atoll's people out for nuclear tests, promising they could return. Marshallese had no words for radiation or fallout. Their first new home, Rongerik, ran out of food; by 1948 they were eating flour-and-water gruel.

3/ Next came tents beside the Kwajalein airport runway. Then, in November 1948, they moved to Kili, their third move in two years. They chose it over a populated atoll because no iroij, or paramount king, ruled it. They have long compared it to a prison.

4/ With no lagoon, fishing is hard and the coral soil is poor, so Kili lives on imported rice, flour and Spam paid for by US compensation. In 2017 local leaders took full control of the trust fund, $59M or over $70M depending on the source. By early 2023 it held $100,000.

post_text: Sulphur fumes stripped the vegetation, typhoid was ever present, and the company decided which workers could rent a house. Copper Cliff, a former company town in Greater Sudbury, Ontario. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ In 1883 Tom Flanagan, a blacksmith building the Canadian Pacific Railway, noticed a rust-coloured patch of rock. The ore went to a smelter in New Jersey, which found it rich in nickel. By 1888 a nickel smelter stood at Copper Cliff, and the town grew around it.

3/ A company town until 1973 (from 1886 or the 1890s; sources differ). Company houses were for Anglo-Saxons only; Poles, Finns and Italians lived in Shantytown. Police were on Inco's payroll. In the Depression a job reportedly meant helping a mine's hockey or soccer team.

4/ The smelter, now Vale's, is still why the town exists. In 1972 Inco finished the Superstack, 381 m tall, to carry its fumes away. Outsiders see a symbol of pollution. Locals see a symbol of who they are.

post_text: In 1930 the last 36 people on St Kilda, the westernmost islands of Scotland's Outer Hebrides, left an open Bible and a pile of oats in every house and sailed away. Their working dogs were drowned in the bay. Why did people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Seabirds. For thousands of years islanders lived on gannets, fulmars and puffins. Breakfast was thin porridge with a puffin boiled in it. One report says each person ate 115 fulmars a year. Men climbed cliffs on ropes, sometimes barefoot, for eggs and young birds.

3/ Every morning the men met in the street as a 'parliament', with no one in charge, to decide the day's work. They were so cut off that soldiers hunting Bonnie Prince Charlie after 1746 found the islanders had never heard of him, or of King George II.

4/ After the First World War most young men left, and in 1930 the last 36 asked to go. In 1955 the British government put St Kilda into a missile-tracking range, and from 1957 it was inhabited year-round again. Defence workers still staff Hirta on rotation.

post_text: For decades, people were sent to this island by law, and its money was not allowed to leave. Culion, an island off the northern tip of Palawan in the Philippines, still has about 24,000 residents. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ In 1904 the American colonial government reserved Culion as a leper colony. Residents were bought out and made to leave. The first patients arrived from Cebu in 1906, and a 1907 law made segregation compulsory. By 1910, 5,303 people with leprosy had been rounded up.

3/ Patients had their own police, a court of fellow lepers and an inmate-financed power company. From 1913 the colony had its own coins: officials feared, with no scientific basis, that ordinary money carried the disease. Patients at first threw the coins into the sea.

4/ After new treatments, patients were paroled by the thousands, and many did not want to leave. Their descendants are part of Culion today. The health department ran it until 1998. Now it is a fishing town where, one resident said, everyone is a fisherman.

post_text: Vardø lies further east than Istanbul, Kyiv and Saint Petersburg, on a small island in the Barents Sea off Norway's far northeast. The sun stays down for about two months, and local lore says the town has exactly one tree. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ It began as a border claim. In the early 1300s King Håkon V built a fortress on the island to assert Norwegian rule and tax the far north, within reach of Russian Novgorod. A settlement grew up under the garrison's protection.

3/ Pomor merchants from Russia's White Sea coast bartered flour and wood for fish, which they needed because the Orthodox fast banned meat. Vardø had Russian bakeries, took the ruble and spoke a Russian-Norwegian trade language. The trade won it a town charter in 1789.

4/ The sea stays ice-free in winter. Fishing and fish processing are still the largest industry. The fortress fires a salute each January when the sun returns. On the hill, the US-Norwegian GLOBUS radar officially tracks space junk. Russia's military calls it a threat.

post_text: For almost 150 years, one family ran these coral atolls as a private fiefdom, paying workers in money it minted itself that only its own store accepted. The Cocos (Keeling) Islands: Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, 5 metres high at most. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Coconuts. In the 1820s two Britons, Alexander Hare and John Clunies-Ross, set out to settle the empty atolls. Hare brought dozens of Malay followers, a volunteer harem in one account and captives in a scholarly one. They drifted to Clunies-Ross, and Hare was gone by 1831.

3/ Clunies-Ross recruited workers from Java, Sumatra, Bali, Papua and beyond to make copra. Paid in Cocos rupees, they could not own land or leave without permission. In 1978, under threat of compulsory acquisition, Australia made the family sell for A$6.25m.

4/ The workers' descendants stayed. About 600 people live there (593 at the 2021 census), mostly Malay-speaking Muslims on Home Island. The government supplies about half the jobs, and most food is imported: a cucumber cost $12 in 2015. The golf course plays across the runway.

post_text: For 104 years a triangle of land smaller than 4 sq km belonged to neither of its neighbours. No army could occupy it, residents had no vote, and it had no currency of its own. Neutral Moresnet, where Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands meet today. Why did people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Zinc. After Napoleon, the Netherlands and Prussia both wanted the Vieille Montagne mine; Bristol was one of the few other places processing zinc. The Congress of Vienna left it unsettled. The 1816 fix: make the mine and its village neutral, pending a future agreement.

3/ The mine company ran the place: housing, shops, a hospital, a bank, schools, even the doctor. Taxes were low, there were no import duties, residents could distil alcohol tax-free, and stateless 'Neutrals' for a time escaped conscription. About 256 people became thousands.

4/ A casino opened in 1903, and in 1908 the mine's doctor proposed making it the first Esperanto state, Amikejo, with an anthem to the tune of 'O Tannenbaum'. Then Versailles gave it to Belgium. In 1920 it became Kelmis, named after the dialect word for zinc spar.

post_text: In 1785 a volcano killed about 130 of the 327 people on this island, and by 1802 nobody was left. Today about 160 people live there again. Aogashima, the southernmost inhabited island of Japan's Izu chain, about 358 km south of mainland Tokyo. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ In 1817, a petition to rebuild was made. An advance party of 20 landed under Sasaki Jirodayu, whom one writer calls "the Moses of Aogashima." By 1834 or 1835 about 240 people had returned, most of them fishers. The villages they formed are the ones that stand today.

3/ One source says residents rely heavily on government assistance; another says about 70 of 170 are government workers on short-term posts. Steam vents called hingya run a free communal cooker and a sauna, and evaporate deep-sea water into Kuroshio Hingya salt.

4/ Getting there is the hard part. About 40% of ferries from Hachijō-jima are canceled, and sometimes none runs for over a week. The helicopter has 9 seats. Every day a loudspeaker tells the village whether the boat is running. When it isn't, residents say: "Not again."

post_text: You can't be buried in Longyearbyen, a town of about 2,400 on Svalbard in the Norwegian Arctic. Burials stopped in 1950, after bodies of 1918 flu victims were found undecayed in the permafrost. The terminally ill are usually sent to the mainland. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Coal. John Munro Longyear, a Michigan businessman, visited Svalbard on a 1901 cruise and saw money in its coal. His Boston-based Arctic Coal Company began mining in 1906, with American managers and mostly Norwegian miners. They called it Longyear City.

3/ In 1916 the Norwegian company Store Norske bought the mines and ran the town, housing included. It even issued its own banknotes, withdrawn from 1980. Private cars weren't allowed until 1982. In the 1990s the state ended the company town and brought in local democracy.

4/ Norwegian coal mining is over: Mine 7, the last Norwegian mine on Svalbard, closed on 30 June 2025. Tourism, research and education keep the town going. There is no welfare, and pregnant women leave weeks before birth. The council says it should not be a lifelong community.
